subject: physics_2

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. The book prints the question as "Explain the impact  parameter ?" with a double space and a space before the question mark; both are tidied here and the wording is unchanged. The book writes the nuclear charge as lowercase ze²; the standard symbol Ze² (Z = atomic number of the nucleus) is used here. Physics hand-checked: b = Ze² cot(θ/2) / [4πε₀(½mv²)] — cot(θ/2) falls as θ rises, so b and θ move in opposite directions, and cot(90°) = 0 gives b = 0 at θ = 180°.

recall_prompt: Define the impact parameter, give its formula, and say what happens for a large b, a small b and b = 0.

steps.label: The definition
lines: Impact parameter:
The impact parameter of an α-particle is the
perpendicular distance of the velocity vector
of the α-particle from the centre of the
nucleus, measured when the α-particle is still
far away from the atom. It is denoted by b.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Three parts: perpendicular distance, of the velocity vector, from the centre of the nucleus.
steps.why: The distance has to be measured far away, before the Coulomb force bends the path. Once the path is curved there is no single straight line to measure from.
common_mistakes: Saying b is the distance of closest approach. That is a different quantity, r₀.
Leaving out "far away from the nucleus". Near the nucleus the path is already bent.

recall.must_convey: That b is the perpendicular distance of the α-particle's velocity vector from the centre of the nucleus, measured far away.
accept: perpendicular distance of the velocity vector
from the centre of the nucleus
when the particle is far away
reject: b equals Z e squared cot theta by two

steps.memory_tip: Extend the incoming straight path; b is how far it misses the nucleus by.

steps.label: The formula
lines: Rutherford found the relation between b and the
scattering angle θ:
Here Z is the atomic number of the nucleus, θ
is the scattering angle, and ½mv² is the
kinetic energy of the α-particle.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Write the formula and then name every symbol in it.
steps.why: The formula holds the whole answer: the cot(θ/2) factor gives the shape of the relation, and the ½mv² in the denominator says a faster α-particle is deflected less for the same b.
common_mistakes: Writing tan(θ/2). The formula carries cot(θ/2).
Dropping the kinetic energy term. b depends on the α-particle's energy as well.

recall.must_convey: That b = Ze² cot(θ/2) divided by 4πε₀ times the kinetic energy ½mv².
accept: Z e squared cot theta by two
half m v squared in the denominator

steps.memory_tip: cot on top, kinetic energy underneath.

steps.label: Large b and small b
lines: 1. If b is large, the α-particle passes far from
the nucleus, the repulsion is weak, θ is small
and the deflection is small.
2. If b is small, the α-particle passes close to
the nucleus, the repulsion is strong, θ is
large and the deflection is large.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Both cases, each with its reason: the strength of the Coulomb repulsion.
steps.why: The Coulomb force falls off as 1/r², so a pass at twice the distance gives a quarter of the force and a much smaller turn. This is why almost all α-particles in Rutherford's experiment went nearly straight through.
common_mistakes: Saying b and θ increase together. They move in opposite directions.
Giving the two cases without the reason. The reason is the strength of the repulsion.

recall.must_convey: That a large b gives a small θ and a small b gives a large θ.
reject: b equals zero gives one eighty degrees

steps.memory_tip: Far pass, small turn; close pass, big turn.

steps.label: The head-on case
lines: 3. If b = 0 the α-particle is aimed straight at
the centre of the nucleus. It slows down, stops
and comes straight back along its own path.

lines.text: b large → θ small · b = 0 → θ = 180°

steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. The extreme case, and the word retraces.
steps.why: This is the case that told Rutherford the nucleus exists: only about one α-particle in 8000 came back, so the positive charge must be packed into a very small volume.
common_mistakes: Writing θ = 90° for a head-on hit. Straight back is 180°.
Saying the α-particle passes through the nucleus. It stops and retraces its path.

recall.must_convey: That b = 0 is a head-on approach and gives θ = 180°, the particle retracing its path.

steps.memory_tip: Aim dead centre and the only way out is straight back — 180°.

insider_note: Four separate things are marked here: the definition, the formula, the two cases, and b = 0 — a paragraph that mixes them loses marks.
